**United Nations peacekeeping** is the deployment of international military, police, and civilian personnel under [United Nations](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations") command to help countries transition from conflict to peace.[[2]](#cite_note-2) Authorized by the [United Nations Security Council](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council "United Nations Security Council") and administered by the [Department of Peace Operations](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Department_of_Peace_Operations "United Nations Department of Peace Operations"), it is one of the principal instruments through which the United Nations addresses threats to international peace and security. It is distinguished from [peacemaking](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peacemaking "Peacemaking"), [peace enforcement](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace_enforcement "Peace enforcement"), and [peacebuilding](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peacebuilding "Peacebuilding"), although these activities may overlap in practice.[[3]](#cite_note-autogenerated1-3)

Peacekeeping is not mentioned in the [United Nations Charter](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charter_of_the_United_Nations "Charter of the United Nations"); it developed during the [Cold War](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War "Cold War") as an improvised response to crises the Security Council was unable to address through the originally planned [collective security](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collective_security "Collective security") provisions. Peacekeeping is governed by three principles: there must be consent of the parties, impartiality, and non-use of force except in self-defense and defense of the mandate.[[4]](#cite_note-:36-4) The mandates of UN peacekeeping missions have expanded significantly over time, from early observer deployments to multidimensional operations which may support complex [peace agreements](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace_treaty "Peace treaty") or protect civilians in active conflicts under [Chapter VII of the UN Charter](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapter_VII_of_the_United_Nations_Charter "Chapter VII of the United Nations Charter"). Peacekeepers may include soldiers, police, and civilian participants; they wear their home countries' uniforms and **Blue Helmets** or **Blue Berets**, which have become synonymous with UN peacekeeping.[[5]](#cite_note-5)

Since 1948, more than two million people from 125 countries have served in 72 UN peacekeeping operations; the forces were collectively awarded the [Nobel Peace Prize](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Peace_Prize "Nobel Peace Prize") in 1988.[[6]](#cite_note-:0-6) As of 2026, eleven operations are active, with a combined budget of $5.66 billion and around 53,000 personnel deployed from 117 countries, the largest contributors being [Nepal](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nepal "Nepal"), [Rwanda](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rwanda "Rwanda"), [Bangladesh](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh "Bangladesh"), [India](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India"), and [Pakistan](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan "Pakistan"). Scholars have found that peacekeeping is associated with reduced conflict recurrence and fewer civilian casualties, although effectiveness varies with the local situation and a mission's mandate.

The current [head of the Department of Peace Operations](about://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Department_of_Peace_Operations#List_of_heads "United Nations Department of Peace Operations") is [Jean-Pierre Lacroix](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Pierre_Lacroix_(diplomat) "Jean-Pierre Lacroix (diplomat)"), who has held the office since 1 April 2017.

## Conceptual foundations

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=United_Nations_peacekeeping&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Conceptual foundations")]

### Non-charter origins

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=United_Nations_peacekeeping&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Non-charter origins")]

The [UN Charter](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charter_of_the_United_Nations "Charter of the United Nations") makes no reference to peacekeeping.[[7]](#cite_note-:11-7) Its framers envisioned a collective security system in which the Security Council, supported by armed forces made available by member states under Article 43 and coordinated through the [Military Staff Committee](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_Staff_Committee "Military Staff Committee") established under Article 47, would respond directly to threats to international peace and security.[[7]](#cite_note-:11-7)[[8]](#cite_note-:12-8) However, this system never functioned as designed due to disagreements between the two sides of the beginning [Cold War](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War "Cold War").[[7]](#cite_note-:11-7)[[9]](#cite_note-:13-9) Peacekeeping subsequently developed as an improvised institutional response to crises which the Security Council wanted to address despite the failure of the original mechanisms.[[7]](#cite_note-:11-7)[[8]](#cite_note-:12-8)

Because peacekeeping had no Charter basis, UN Secretary-General [Dag Hammarskjöld](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dag_Hammarskjöld "Dag Hammarskjöld") described it as a "Chapter Six and a Half" activity, situated between the peaceful dispute settlement mandated under Chapter VI, and the military measures authorized under Chapter VII.[[10]](#cite_note-:29-10)[[11]](#cite_note-11) The phrase has remained the standard shorthand for peacekeeping's legal and operational position, and its emergence from the necessity of working around the Charter's practical limits.[[8]](#cite_note-:12-8)

UN peacekeeping follows three core principles, first articulated by Hammarskjöld in 1958[[12]](#cite_note-12) and subsequently codified in the 2008 *UN Peacekeeping Operations: Principles and Guidelines*, commonly known as the Capstone Doctrine.[[3]](#cite_note-autogenerated1-3)[[4]](#cite_note-:36-4) These principles are:

1. Peacekeepers must be deployed with the **consent of the parties** to the conflict, who must be committed to a political process. Without such consent, an operation risks becoming a party to the conflict and being drawn toward enforcement action.[[3]](#cite_note-autogenerated1-3)[[4]](#cite_note-:36-4)
2. Peacekeepers must exhibit **impartiality**, implementing their mandate without favour or prejudice to any party. Impartiality is not equivalent to neutrality: a peacekeeping operation may penalize infractions of the peace process while remaining impartial in its dealings with the parties.[[3]](#cite_note-autogenerated1-3)[[4]](#cite_note-:36-4)
3. Peacekeepers must **not use force except in self-defense, and in defense of the mandate**.[[4]](#cite_note-:36-4) They are generally not an offensive force, but are allowed to proactively deter forceful attempts to disrupt their mandate in what is called "robust peacekeeping".[[3]](#cite_note-autogenerated1-3)

The three principles are interdependent and have been stretched (particularly the third) by the demands of post-Cold War deployments.[[9]](#cite_note-:13-9) The Security Council, even when authorizing robust mandates under Chapter VII, regularly reaffirms them in operative paragraphs of mission resolutions.[[3]](#cite_note-autogenerated1-3)[[9]](#cite_note-:13-9)

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=United_Nations_peacekeeping&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Distinction from other activities")]

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

**Confidence-building measures** (**CBMs**) or **confidence- and security-building measures** (**CSBMs**) are actions taken to reduce fear of attack by both (or more) parties in a situation of conflict.[[1]](#cite_note-Maiese2003_confbuilding_measures-1) The term is most often used in the context of armed conflict, but is similar in logic to that of [trust](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trust_(sociology) "Trust (sociology)") and [interpersonal communication](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interpersonal_communication "Interpersonal communication") used to reduce conflictual situations among human individuals.[[1]](#cite_note-Maiese2003_confbuilding_measures-1)

### Embassies and people to people contacts

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Confidence-building_measures&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Embassies and people to people contacts")]

Confidence-building measures between [sovereign states](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sovereign_state "Sovereign state") for many centuries included the existence of and increased activities by [embassies](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embassy "Embassy"), which are state institutions geographically located inside the territory of other states, staffed by people expected to have extremely good [interpersonal skills](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interpersonal_relations "Interpersonal relations") who can explain and resolve misunderstandings due to differences in language and culture which are incorrectly perceived as threatening, or encourage local knowledge of a foreign culture by funding artistic and cultural activities.

A much more [grassroots](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grassroots "Grassroots") form of confidence building occurs directly between ordinary people of different states. Short visits by individual children or groups of children to another state, and longer visits (6–12 months) by secondary and tertiary students to another state, have widely been used in the [European Union](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union") as one of the methods of decreasing the tensions which had earlier led to many centuries of inter-European wars, culminating in the first and second [world wars](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I").

The use of confidence-building measures (CBMs) as an explicit security management approach emerged from attempts by the [Cold War](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War "Cold War") superpowers and their military alliances (the [North Atlantic Treaty Organization](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NATO "NATO") and the [Warsaw Pact](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warsaw_Pact "Warsaw Pact")), as well as the European neutral and non-aligned states, to avoid conventional or nuclear war by accident or miscalculation.[[2]](#cite_note-CSBMs_Canadian_perspective_1984-2) The term appears to have been first used[[2]](#cite_note-CSBMs_Canadian_perspective_1984-2): 20 in [United Nations General Assembly resolution](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_General_Assembly_resolution "United Nations General Assembly resolution") 914 (x) in 1955,[[3]](#cite_note-UNGARes_914X-3) prompted by the U.S. "Open Skies" proposal. CBMs became a significant component of arms control during a series of negotiations and agreements produced by the [Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conference_on_Security_and_Co-operation_in_Europe "Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe") (CSCE; which later become the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe, OSCE) of the early 1970s.[[2]](#cite_note-CSBMs_Canadian_perspective_1984-2): 28–29 CBMs were a major component of the Helsinki Final Act Document (August 1975), the Stockholm CSBM Document (September 1986), and the [Vienna Document](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienna_Document "Vienna Document") (November 1990) and its iterations of 1992, 1994, 1999, and 2011.[[4]](#cite_note-USStateDept_Overview_ViennaDoc2011-4) Other CBMs during the Cold War included Latin American joint military manoeuvres and exchanges of military observers, with a meeting on 8 January 1984 of Central American states agreeing to set up a detailed registry of military installations, weapons and personnel and methods of direct communication; and the 1975 [Sinai Interim Agreement](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinai_Interim_Agreement "Sinai Interim Agreement") between Israel and Egypt. There are also other historical instances of what appears to be confidence building prior to the Cold War and outside of the European context.[[2]](#cite_note-CSBMs_Canadian_perspective_1984-2): 23–24

## Role of confidence-building measures

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Confidence-building_measures&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Role of confidence-building measures")]

In international relations, the way that confidence-building measures are intended to reduce fear and suspicion (the positive [feedbacks](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feedback "Feedback")) is to make the different states' (or opposition groups') behaviour more predictable. This typically involves exchanging information and making it possible to verify this information, especially information regarding armed forces and military equipment. Here, "positive" and "negative" refer to the mathematical nature of the feedback; positive feedback leads to worsening intensity in a conflict, while negative feedback leads to de-escalation of the conflict, a "peace spiral" or [Gradual Reduction in Tension](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gradual_Reduction_in_Tension?action=edit&redlink=1 "Gradual Reduction in Tension (page does not exist)") (GRIT).[[1]](#cite_note-Maiese2003_confbuilding_measures-1)

More in-depth [modelling of peace and armed conflict situations](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_system_approach_to_peace_and_armed_conflict "Complex system approach to peace and armed conflict") as [complex](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_system "Complex system") [dynamical systems](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamical_system "Dynamical system") suggests that [intractable long-term armed conflict](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protracted_social_conflict "Protracted social conflict") can be interpreted as the result of the reduced dimensionality of a system, in which the system is changing but remains near an [attractor](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attractor "Attractor") that maintains the conflict. The existing negative and positive feedbacks prevent a change to a state of peace. Confidence-building measures can change the properties of the system, increasing its dimensionality, so that in the higher dimensional system, positive feedback loops to resolve the conflict are able to overcome the negative feedbacks that tend to maintain the conflict.[[5]](#cite_note-Coleman2011_Navigating-5): 47–52

### Validity of the model in the Internet era

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Confidence-building_measures&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Validity of the model in the Internet era")]

If the [feedback](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feedback "Feedback") model assumed by the confidence-building measure mechanism is correct, then the rapidly developing improvement in communication between ordinary people by the [internet](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet "Internet") should provide extremely robust, fast methods of information exchange and verification, as well as improved people-to-people contacts and general building of [trust](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trust_(sociology) "Trust (sociology)") networks, reducing the intensity and frequency of [wars](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War "War"). Evidence, however, suggests that the Internet is as likely to inflame opinion and increase conflict (or at least tensions) as individuals are exposed to significantly different points of view.

## Typology of confidence-building measures

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Confidence-building_measures&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Typology of confidence-building measures")]

Existing and proposed confidence-building measures in the context of [arms control](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arms_control "Arms control"), also called *confidence and security-building measures* (CSBMs), can be categorized by three main types. Confidence building can also be [viewed as an overall process](#Confidence_building_viewed_as_a_process), rather than a collection of individual measures. In a monograph distributed to the [Conference on Disarmament](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conference_on_Disarmament "Conference on Disarmament") in 1997,[[6]](#cite_note-UNDigLib_Macintosh96_distrib-6) Macintosh divides CSBMs into informational type (A), verification type (B) and constraint (C) measures.[[7]](#cite_note-Macintosh_confbuilding_transformation-7)

### Type A: Information, interaction, and communication measures

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Confidence-building_measures&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Type A: Information, interaction, and communication measures")]

Informational and similar type measures include:[[7]](#cite_note-Macintosh_confbuilding_transformation-7)

1. *Information* measures: measures requiring or encouraging the provision (exchange) of information about military forces, facilities, structures, and activities. Examples include: publication of defence information; weapon system and force structure information exchange; consultative commissions; publication of defence budget figures; and publication of weapon system development information.
2. *Experience* measures: measures requiring or encouraging the opportunity to interact with officials or experts from other countries. Examples include: military personnel exchanges; security expert exchanges; transnational secondments; joint military training and joint military exercises; and seminars discussing doctrine, strategy, and technology issues.

The [Prime Minister of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_India "Prime Minister of India"), [Narendra Modi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Narendra_Modi "Narendra Modi") meeting the [Chinese leader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramount_leader "Paramount leader"), [Xi Jinping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xi_Jinping "Xi Jinping"), in [Wuhan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wuhan "Wuhan"), China during a [Shanghai Cooperation Organisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghai_Cooperation_Organisation "Shanghai Cooperation Organisation") [summit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Tianjin_SCO_summit "2025 Tianjin SCO summit") on 31 August 2025

[China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China") and [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India") maintained peaceful relations for thousands of years, but their relationship has varied since the [Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party") (CCP)'s victory in the [Chinese Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Civil_War "Chinese Civil War") in 1949 and the [annexation of Tibet by the People's Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annexation_of_Tibet_by_the_People's_Republic_of_China "Annexation of Tibet by the People's Republic of China"). The two nations have sought economic cooperation with each other, while frequent border disputes and [economic nationalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_nationalism "Economic nationalism") in both countries are major points of contention.

Cultural and economic relations between China and India date back to ancient times. The [Silk Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silk_Road "Silk Road") not only served as a major [trade route](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trade_route "Trade route") between India and China, but is also credited for facilitating the spread of [Buddhism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddhism "Buddhism") from India to East Asia.[[1]](#cite_note-Maria-1) During the 19th century, the British [East India Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company "East India Company") increasingly [exported opium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opium_trade_in_China "Opium trade in China"), grown in India, leading to the [Opium Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opium_Wars "Opium Wars").[[2]](#cite_note-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Sen2003-3) During [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), both [British India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Raj "British Raj") and the [Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_China_(1912%E2%80%931949) "Republic of China (1912–1949)") (ROC) played a crucial role in halting the progress of [Imperial Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_Japan "Imperial Japan").[[4]](#cite_note-Barbara-4) After India became independent in 1947, it established relations with the ROC. The modern Sino-Indian diplomatic relationship began in 1950, when India was among the first noncommunist countries to end formal relations with the [Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_China "Republic of China") and recognise the PRC as the legitimate government of both [Mainland China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_China "Mainland China") and [Taiwan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Taiwan "Geography of Taiwan"). China and India are two of the major [regional powers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regional_power "Regional power") in Asia, and are the two [most populous countries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_population "List of countries by population") and among the [fastest growing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_real_GDP_growth_rate "List of countries by real GDP growth rate") major economies in the world.

Growth in diplomatic and economic influence has increased the significance of their bilateral relationship. Between 2008 and 2021, China was India's largest trading partner, and the two countries have extended their strategic and military relations.[[5]](#cite_note-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6)[[7]](#cite_note-Hindu1-7)[[8]](#cite_note-NDTV-8) India has a large [trade deficit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trade_deficit "Trade deficit") that is favoured towards China. The [Sino-Indian border dispute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sino-Indian_border_dispute "Sino-Indian border dispute"), manifested by the [Line of Actual Control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_of_Actual_Control "Line of Actual Control") (LAC), remains a central issue, resulting in the 1962 [Sino-Indian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sino-Indian_War "Sino-Indian War"), the [clashes in 1967](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathu_La_and_Cho_La_clashes "Nathu La and Cho La clashes"), and the [a standoff in 1987](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1987_Sino-Indian_skirmish "1987 Sino-Indian skirmish").[[9]](#cite_note-APCSS-9) Since the late 1980s, both countries have rebuilt diplomatic and economic ties; a 1996 agreement forbids firearms and explosives near the LAC.[[10]](#cite_note-10)

Border deconfliction mechanisms emerged, beginning with the 2003 [Special Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_Representative_mechanism_on_the_India%E2%80%93China_boundary_question "Special Representative mechanism on the India–China boundary question"). Renewed conflicts included [standoffs in 2013](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_Depsang_standoff "2013 Depsang standoff"), and [in 2017](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_China%E2%80%93India_border_standoff "2017 China–India border standoff"); [major skirmishes in 2020-2021](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020%E2%80%932021_China%E2%80%93India_skirmishes "2020–2021 China–India skirmishes") resulted in dozens of deaths on both sides; military infrastructure near the LAC continues to grow.[[11]](#cite_note-WSJ-11)[[12]](#cite_note-12) India's concerns include China's [close relations with Pakistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China%E2%80%93Pakistan_relations "China–Pakistan relations"),[[13]](#cite_note-13) and with [separatist groups in Northeast India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insurgency_in_Northeast_India "Insurgency in Northeast India").[[14]](#cite_note-14) China's concerns include Indian military and economic activities in the disputed [South China Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_China_Sea "South China Sea")[[15]](#cite_note-15) and hosting of [Tibetan exiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibetan_exile "Tibetan exile").[[16]](#cite_note-16)[[17]](#cite_note-17) Today, South Asia is the primary site of [great power competition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_power_competition "Great power competition") between China and India.[[18]](#cite_note-18)

## Geopolitical overview

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=China%E2%80%93India_relations&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Geopolitical overview")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e5/Sino-Indian_Geography.png/330px-Sino-Indian_Geography.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sino-Indian_Geography.png)

Eastern and Southern Asia. 

---

(The border between the People's Republic of China and the India over [Arunachal Pradesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arunachal_Pradesh "Arunachal Pradesh")/[South Tibet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Tibet "South Tibet") reflects actual control, without dotted line showing claims.)

The China–India border straddles the [Himalayas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Himalayas "Himalayas"), with [Nepal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nepal "Nepal") and [Bhutan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhutan "Bhutan") acting as [buffer states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buffer_state "Buffer state"). The **Special Representative mechanism on the India–China boundary question** (**SR**/**SRM**) was constituted in 2003 to "explore from the political perspective of the overall bilateral relationship the framework of a boundary settlement". [Atal Bihari Vajpayee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atal_Bihari_Vajpayee "Atal Bihari Vajpayee"), in the capacity of [Minister of External Affairs of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_of_External_Affairs_(India) "Minister of External Affairs (India)"), had first suggested the SR mechanism during his visit to China in 1979.[[1]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeepak202065-1) During another visit to China by Vajpayee, this time in the capacity of [Prime Minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_India "Prime Minister of India"), in June 2003, the mechanism was mentioned in an agreement between the two countries. The latest mention of the SR mechanism was in a joint press statement between India and China on 10 September 2020.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeepak202065–68-2)[[3]](#cite_note-3)

During the 4th round of talks in 2004, [Dai Bingguo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dai_Bingguo "Dai Bingguo") suggested that the SR mechanism follow a 3 step formula for the settlement of the India–China boundary question:[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeepak202065–68-2)

1. Establish the political parameters and guiding principles
2. Establish the framework for a final package settlement
3. Delineate and demarcate the boundary

The first step was completed with the [Agreement on the Political Parameters and Guiding Principles for the Settlement of the India–China Boundary Question](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agreement_on_the_Political_Parameters_and_Guiding_Principles_for_the_Settlement_of_the_India%E2%80%93China_Boundary_Question,_2005 "Agreement on the Political Parameters and Guiding Principles for the Settlement of the India–China Boundary Question, 2005") being signed in 2005.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeepak202065–68-2) The second phase of negotiations began with the sixth round of talks.[[4]](#cite_note-4)

During the 15th round of the SR talks in 2012, the [Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_Mechanism_for_Consultation_and_Coordination_on_India%E2%80%93China_Border_Affairs "Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination on India–China Border Affairs") was set up.[[5]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPanda201743-5)

# Lens 2B.7 — Xi Jinping (China), 2023

**Question:** Did the ruler pursue credible ceasefires, peace talks, confidence-building measures, lawful settlements, or post-conflict reconciliation when possible?

**One-sentence answer for 2023:** The 2023 record is **mixed but weighted negative** — Xi executed one real 2023 CBM (the March 2023 Iran–Saudi rapprochement; the November 2023 mil-to-mil reset) and maintained the bilateral India border architecture, but did **not** pursue credible ceasefires, peace talks, or lawful settlements on the active 2023 dispute theaters (Taiwan, South China Sea, LAC, Hong Kong NSL, Xinjiang). The persistence of grey-zone coercion in active theaters without settlement frameworks is the dominant 2023 pattern.

---

## A. Claim-level findings — CBM and settlement positives

### 1. March 2023 Iran–Saudi rapprochement (China-brokered, real CBM)

## C. Net reading for lens 2B.7

The 2023 evidence is **mixed** but weighted negative on the question of credible ceasefires, peace talks, CBMs, lawful settlements, or post-conflict reconciliation:

- **Positive CBMs (real but narrow):** Iran–Saudi rapprochement (March 2023); mil-to-mil reset (November 2023); NFU reaffirmation; India border architecture held; no new kinetic war in 2023.
- **Negative settlements (the dominant 2023 pattern):** Taiwan — no peace talk, no settlement framework, continued grey-zone coercion; South China Sea — no binding COC, no settlement, continued grey-zone coercion; India LAC — no 2023 disengagement, no progress; Hong Kong — NSL trials continued, no settlement framework with pro-democracy camp; Xinjiang — no settlement, no independent inspection, "success" framing; arms-control — no engagement; proxy allies — no partner correction; civil society — no internal-restraint CBMs.

A ruler scoring well on this lens would have (a) used the November 2023 Biden–Xi summit as a platform for cross-strait crisis-management framework, (b) accepted a binding South China Sea COC, (c) completed a 2023 India LAC disengagement, (d) paused the Hong Kong 47 trial pending a settlement framework, (e) opened Xinjiang to OHCHR follow-up, (f) ratified the CTBT, (g) conditioned the Iran / Pakistan / Syria / Russia partnerships on CBM engagement, and (h) released political prisoners. Xi did none of these.

**Net judgment: 2B.7 reads as mixed-to-negative for 2023 — Xi executed two real CBMs (Iran–Saudi, mil-to-mil) and maintained the India architecture, but did not pursue credible ceasefires, peace talks, or lawful settlements on the active 2023 dispute theaters. The pattern is consistent with a ruler for whom CBMs are tactical tools (de-escalation for individual foreign-policy gains) rather than a commitment to a comprehensive settlement framework.**
